chunks: Wide-bandgap semiconductors: SiC, GaN. The question: What novel semiconductors are being explored for power electronics? What are their tradeoffs?
Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) are semiconductors with a much wider "bandgap" than silicon.
That lets a power transistor made from them block high voltage while being thinner.
The result is less resistance and faster switching than silicon, so power converters can be smaller and more efficient.
Think of a dam holding back water. A stronger material lets you build a thinner wall for the same height of water.
In a power transistor, the "wall" is a layer that blocks voltage.
Wide-bandgap materials withstand about ten times the electric field, so that layer can be much thinner, and the current has a shorter path through it when the transistor is on.
The dam picture breaks down on cost: the new materials are pricier.
Each material follows R on sp proportional to V B squared , but the lines are separated by orders of magnitude because of E c to the 3 .
At a given V B , SiC and GaN sit about 300-1000 times below silicon.
These are theoretical limits for the drift region only; real devices are well above them, and silicon superjunction closes some of the gap at 600-900 volts.
Bandgap: the energy an electron needs to jump into a conducting state. It is measured in electron-volts (eV): silicon is 1. 12 eV, and SiC and GaN are about 3. 3 eV.
Breakdown field: the most voltage per unit of thickness (electric field) a material can take before it fails. On-resistance: the resistance of a transistor when it is on.
Lower means less heat. Switching loss: energy wasted each time the transistor turns on or off. dv/dt, di/dt: how fast voltage and current change. Higher with these devices.
Compare two transistors rated for the same voltage. The silicon one needs a thick blocking layer.
The SiC or GaN one needs about a tenth as thick, so it has far lower on-resistance and much less capacitance to charge.
Less resistance means less conduction heat, and less capacitance means faster, cheaper switching. That is the whole idea.
"The main ones are silicon carbide and gallium nitride, with gallium oxide and diamond in research.
Their wide bandgap gives a critical field about ten times silicon's, so the drift region can be much thinner.
That gives much lower on-resistance for a given voltage, smaller capacitances and faster switching, so higher efficiency and frequency with smaller magnetics.
SiC fits high voltage, GaN fits up to roughly 650 volts and MHz.
The trade-offs are cost, gate drive constraints, reliability maturity and layout sensitivity because of very fast edges."
